items.originalTitle: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
items.author: VicOne
items.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
items.summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “ Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .”

items.originalTitle: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey
items.author: Temi Wilkey
items.title: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey
items.summary: Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost . The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died. Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community alive. No – she was prophesying 40 years into the future about the digital-age phenomenon of ghosting. The fact that this practice is widespread enough for there to be a word for it is proof of the long since disintegrated fabric of our society. Temi Wilkey is a writer, performer and star of the one-woman shows Main Character Energy and Lover Girl , which is at the Soho theatre, London from 2 to 21 November

items.originalTitle: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.author: Sam Leith
items.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.summary: Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14. So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

items.originalTitle: Woman’s kratom addiction spiraled from 4 capsules to 100 a day: ‘Zombie shell of myself’
items.title: Woman’s kratom addiction spiraled from 4 capsules to 100 a day: ‘Zombie shell of myself’
items.summary: Kratom-related reports to U.S. poison centers rose about 1,200% from 2015 to 2025, reaching a record high of 3,434 last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For Hilary Tesluck, a 30-year-old woman in Michigan, the potential for addiction began well before those numbers emerged. Tesluck, who now works to raise awareness of kratom addiction and support others in recovery, said she first tried kratom capsules in 2017 at age 21. KRATOM INDUSTRY WARNS SYNTHETIC OPIOIDS SHOULD NOT BE CALLED 'KRATOM' Her initial use involved leaf kratom rather than concentrated 7-OH products , she shared. The American Kratom Association argues that 7-OH should be distinguished from natural leaf kratom, while acknowledging that kratom itself can cause dependence. "It was introduced to me by a friend who knew that I was someone who suffered from anxiety and took prescription medication for it," Tesluck told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be more holistic and natural in what I was consuming." She noted that she doesn’t recall any dosing recommendations on the label. "I didn’t know how much to take, but my friend told me to take four capsules." WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS At first, Tesluck – an undergraduate student at the time, who was also conducting research and tutoring – noticed the substance gave her a boost in energy, confidence and productivity. Tesluck's daily intake climbed gradually. "Very slowly, over time, I had to take just one more capsule or just one more dose, and then went all the way up to 100," she said. Her day-to-day functioning began to suffer, she shared. "I was not doing very well at work. I was getting … written up for performance." Physically, she had lost nearly 40 pounds and struggled to even stand in the shower "because my body was so wasted away." Tesluck’s belief that kratom was natural and legal made her growing dependence difficult to accept, she said. "About a year and a half into my kratom addiction from just the leaf … I finally realized I needed to do something, and I needed help." When she first sought treatment in 2020, Tesluck described feeling dismissed, saying that the facility’s urine test did not detect her use and that she had to explain what kratom was to the staff. "They were confused why I was there," she said. "So I left after just a few days because I felt kind of humiliated, and I went right back to my use." Tesluck found more help in 2021, when she attended an online recovery meeting. "I had nothing to lose," she said. "It changed everything for me to hear other people telling my story for the first time." After years of feeling alone in her addiction , she said, she finally felt surrounded by people who understood. In 2023, Tesluck relapsed following her grandmother’s death. "I was just grief-stricken. She was really close to me," she said. "So I went to the smoke shop just to get a little bit of kratom, just one time." She later experienced a separate relapse involving 7-OH , which she said followed the death of her cat and the end of a relationship on the same night. MEN AND WOMEN WHO SMOKE MARIJUANA MAY EXPERIENCE DIFFERENT EFFECTS, STUDY SUGGESTS 7-OH, short for 7-hydroxymitragynine, occurs naturally in trace amounts in kratom. Concentrated 7-OH products contain much higher levels than the leaf itself. The body converts some of kratom’s main active compound, mitragynine, into 7-OH, research shows. Both compounds act on opioid receptors and can contribute to dependence, according to the FDA. "The 7-OH was very strong," Tesluck said. "I stayed on that for just a few months because of how intense it was." She returned to her recovery group for support. "I had to take a leave of absence, and I got clean from 7-OH again with their help," she said. Having struggled with both leaf kratom and 7-OH, Tesluck views them as closely connected. "It’s one problem at two strengths," she said. ‘SUPER-DRUG’ 10 TIMES STRONGER THAN FENTANYL LINKED TO DEATHS ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy for the American Kratom Association, disputed this characterization of leaf kratom and concentrated 7-OH. In comments to Fox News Digital, he argued that the body’s conversion of mitragynine into 7-OH does not produce equivalent exposure to concentrated products. Haddow also raised the possibility that the capsules Tesluck initially consumed may have contained ingredients beyond natural leaf kratom. Kratom rules vary widely across the country, with states taking different approaches to age restrictions, product standards and bans. "It’s really been a patchwork," Tesluck said. "It’s different from state to state. Some states ban it, some states regulate it." Florida, for example, prohibits selling or providing kratom products to anyone under 21. Washington’s health department says unscheduled kratom products remain largely unregulated there, without age restrictions, labeling standards or ingredient-testing requirements. Texas law requires kratom product labels to include directions and a recommended serving size. Haddow also emphasized the need for consumer warnings, adding, "The American Kratom Association supports accurate labeling to warn consumers that kratom can cause dependence." "We support stronger enforcement across the board, and excise taxes on kratom products to fund that enforcement." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER In an October interview with Fox News Digital, Haddow also backed age restrictions. "Twenty-one and up should be the only people who have access to these products," he said. Tesluck also raised concerns about how the products are marketed, describing social media ads as looking "very harmless" or "very cool," potentially drawing consumers’ interest. "It’s something that you might want to try just based on the marketing itself and the packaging," she warned. Tesluck said her work regularly brings her into contact with parents grieving children whose deaths they attribute to kratom products, including in states with Kratom Consumer Protection Acts. The FDA says no kratom drugs are approved by the agency, and that kratom cannot legally be marketed as a dietary supplement or added to conventional foods. In December 2025, federal authorities seized approximately 73,000 concentrated 7-OH products valued at roughly $1 million from three Missouri firms, according to the FDA. People taking kratom should pay attention to whether their use is beginning to dictate their daily routines, including planning around obtaining it or worrying about running out, Tesluck urged. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Like making sure when the smoke shop closes that you have enough time to get there," she said. Diminished appetite, weight loss and hair loss were among the effects Tesluck experienced. Other signs of problematic kratom use may include cravings, higher consumption than intended, unsuccessful attempts to stop, and continued use despite problems at work or home, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Feeling unable to miss a dose was another concern for Tesluck. "If I took less than what I was taking, I would feel even worse and sicker," she recalled. "So I was kind of stuck at that baseline with kratom." Haddow acknowledged that consumers can develop dependence or addiction. "Kratom can cause physical dependence, and some consumers have reported they develop addiction to kratom," he told Fox News Digital. Feelings of sedation, numbness or irritability may also occur, Tesluck said. "I was kind of like a zombie shell of myself overall," she said. "I wasn’t really the same person, personality-wise. I was irritable. I was mean." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Today, Tesluck describes herself as a "person in long-term recovery from both kratom and 7-OH addiction." She serves as executive director of End Kratom Addiction, a Virginia-based nonprofit that aims to raise awareness of kratom-related risks and advocates for stronger regulation. "My advocacy looks a lot like meeting one-on-one with families … and coordinating resources for those who are still in addiction," she said.

items.originalTitle: Cuba’s rulers can shout at diplomats. They cannot silence the cry for freedom
items.title: Cuba’s rulers can shout at diplomats. They cannot silence the cry for freedom
items.summary: The world is beginning to push back against the propaganda Havana has peddled for decades at the United Nations as the corruption, oppression, and hypocrisy of its Communist rulers are exposed for all to see. But there is more work to do. Havana’s regime cronies are desperate to survive in the face of growing international pressure, and the free world must continue to confront their lies and expose their corruption until they no longer hold power. For the first time in 31 years, under the leadership of President Trump, a third of the world declined to support Havana’s sham anti-embargo resolution at the UN. 63 nations refused to vote with the Cuban regime, more than double last year’s number. By way of comparison: only two countries voted against Cuba during all four years of the Biden administration — and the U.S. even voted with Cuba under Obama. TRUMP EXPANDS CUBA SANCTIONS BEYOND US COMPANIES IN MAJOR CRACKDOWN ON FOREIGN ENABLERS Two weeks ago, I stood before the General Assembly and asked Cuba’s robber-barons a few simple questions. Why do they wear Rolexes while their people struggle to buy groceries? Why do their families have yachts and private islands while hospitals run out of medicine? Why does their military conglomerate control billions while ordinary Cubans sit in the dark? The regime’s "diplomats" responded by pounding their desks, shouting, and trying to intimidate me. Their Foreign Minister marched toward the podium. And their First Secretary confronted an American diplomat who discovered that the Cubans were trying to get the UN to cut my microphone. SHOUTING MATCH ERUPTS AT UN AS CUBAN FOREIGN MINISTER MOVES TOWARD US AMBASSADOR'S PODIUM: 'BACK UP!' They had plenty of theatrics and outrage. But not a single answer. And this is what I told the Assembly: If this is how the regime acts at the UN in a room full of diplomats, just imagine how they treat people on the island who bravely speak out. So, what are they so afraid of? MIKE WALTZ REVEALS CUBAN DIPLOMAT SHOVED US STAFFER, SLAPPED PHONE AWAY IN EXPLOSIVE UN CLASH For 67 years, the Castro regime has blamed America for the suffering it has inflicted on its own people. When Fidel Castro seized power, he confiscated businesses and farms, sent his opponents before firing squads, and shipped them to forced-labor camps. Generations fled across the Florida Straits and so many more never made it out. Today, thanks to the regime, families endure blackouts lasting days . Hospitals lack basic medicine. And more than 800 political prisoners languish behind bars. CUBA PLUNGES INTO TOTAL BLACKOUT AS ELECTRICAL GRID COLLAPSES AGAIN, US EMBASSY WARNS During October 28th’s proceedings, José Daniel Ferrer (who was imprisoned, released, and then imprisoned again for demanding freedom) joined me at the General Assembly, watching from the gallery. The week before, I hosted another recently freed political prisoner at the UN, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara, who spent five years behind bars for advocating for freedom and creating art the regime didn’t like. These are the Cubans the world should be listening to. Their message: the world stands with the regime every time it votes for Cuba’s "embargo" resolution. TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS And then there’s the money. Investigative reporting by the Miami Herald's Nora Gámez Torres exposed financial records of GAESA , Cuba's military-run conglomerate. The records suggested $18 billion in current assets, including $14.5 billion in financial accounts. That $14.5 billion could cover every single Cuban’s salary for two years straight. It could buy 2 billion gallons of gasoline at Havana prices. Or, it could even stock every single Cuban pharmacy for 43 years at the regime’s own projected costs. The regime pockets billions more from the wholesale confiscation of wages taken from the nurses, doctors, and soldiers it sends around the world. If they don’t cooperate, the regime threatens their families. I WAS LUCKY ENOUGH TO ESCAPE CUBAN SOCIALISM. AMERICA’S 250TH REMINDS ME WHY Meanwhile, the Castro family enjoys exclusive compounds, luxury yachts, and a private island retreat complete with a marina and dolphin lagoon. Fidel famously wore two Rolexes. His descendants vacation in Europe while ordinary Cubans risk their lives trying to escape. Instead of answering for any of this, Havana cries "blockade." But, there is no American naval cordon around Cuba. Ships arrive from dozens of countries around the world. In the first eight months of 2026, American businesses exported more than $876 million in goods to Cuba. That includes $231.7 million in fuel — so much fuel, in fact, that the U.S. is now the largest supplier of fuel to Cuba’s private sector. Naturally, the regime objects to that very phrase: "private sector." But that’s precisely the point. American fuel should power a Cuban farmer’s tractor instead of a Castro grandson’s BMW. And American medicine should reach sick children instead of disappearing into the hands of Cuban elites. Since 1992, the regime has used this vote in the UN General Assembly as a layup against America—and against its own people. Every year, it parades the vote before the Cuban people on state TV to propagate the lie that the world stands with the regime, that Havana is the victim, and that America is to blame for the Cuban people’s misery. In 2024, only 3 countries voted no or abstained. This year, that number is over 60 countries strong and growing as we continue to expose the regime’s corruption and oppression. So, here’s my challenge to every freedom-loving nation — and to every American who believes the Cuban people deserve better: keep demanding answers about the stolen billions, the prisoners still in jail, and the corruption in plain sight. And when the regime demands your pity, remember the suffering of its people and the opulence it wants you to ignore. The Cuban people will be free. And I pray they finally taste freedom on President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s watch. Cuba Libre.

items.title: NFL Week 10 Sunday takeaways: Bengals look unbeatable, Chiefs are scary again, DeMeco Ryans is on the hot seat
items.summary: The NFL gave us another Sunday full of reasons to change our minds. Some teams are making it easier to believe in them, while others are making it harder to remember why we ever did. I'll try to make sense of it all, which is a generous description of what usually happens in this column. Here's my biggest takeaway from each game on the Week 10 Sunday slate. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Takeaway: The Patriots' season is over. That might seem harsh for a team at 5-5 and still very much in the playoff picture, but New England is coming off a Super Bowl appearance, and any hope of a repeat trip is dead. Drake Maye left with an ankle injury, A.J. Brown was hurt again, and the defense is a complete disaster. New England benefited from a weaker AFC last season due to injuries to several star quarterbacks. This year’s path looks considerably tougher. Buffalo, Cincinnati and Kansas City are just way better than New England. Thus, the season is over. Takeaway: The Purple People Eaters are back. It's not often that I admit when I'm wrong, but I left the Vikings off my list of serious Super Bowl contenders after Week 9. I didn't think the offense, even after the Kirk Cousins trade, was good enough. But it might not matter. One week after the Packers scored 45 points against the Patriots, the Vikings made Green Bay's offensive line look like it was playing a man down. Jordan Love had never been sacked more than five times in a game. Minnesota finished with eight, all before the fourth quarter even started. With a defense like that, the offense simply needs to be competent. And it looked plenty competent with Cousins on Sunday at Lambeau. Takeaway: The Jaguars did what they were supposed to do. Jacksonville is the media darling in the AFC, with many suggesting this team is a Super Bowl contender. I'm still not buying it. Look, they did what they were supposed to do on Sunday: go into Tennessee and beat up on a clearly inferior team. Good for them. But to me, the Jags have only one quality win this season: their victory over the Bengals. Other than that, they've feasted on a very easy schedule while playing in a weak division. I still want to see this team against tougher competition, so I'm looking forward to their trip to Chicago to face the Bears on Dec. 6. Takeaway: The Kansas City Chiefs are as dangerous as ever. I'm not going to go overboard praising the Chiefs for beating the Falcons, but there were a couple of key developments beyond the final score. The first is that new addition Josh Downs fit seamlessly into the offense and made a nice touchdown grab. The second is that the Chiefs clearly have two talented and explosive running backs. With Kenneth Walker out with a groin injury, Emmett Johnson balled out with 171 total yards and two touchdowns. One thing that held the Chiefs back last season was a lack of playmakers on offense. Well, they added Walker in free agency, drafted Johnson and traded for Downs. Suddenly, the cupboard is very full in Kansas City. And that should be scary for the rest of the NFL. Takeaway: I can't wait for Thanksgiving night. What else is there to say? The Jets stink and the Bills are elite. We already knew both of these things. The key, though, is that Buffalo really hasn't been tested this season. Their lone loss came against a Patriots team that doesn't look very good. Their two best wins came against the Lions and Rams, but neither team was playing as well then as it is now. Yes, they beat the Vikings, but Minnesota started Carson Wentz . ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Nothing changes next week when Buffalo hosts Miami. But then the Chiefs come to town on Thanksgiving night for what could be the swing game in the battle for the No. 1 seed in the AFC. Get your popcorn ready. Takeaway: Bad teams find ways to lose. To be fair to Miami, it's better to lose and set yourself up for a better draft pick than to win games at this point. And give Jeff Hafley credit: the Dolphins are playing hard for their rookie head coach. But this was a game they really should have won. Miami outgained Indianapolis, had more first downs and won the turnover battle. But kicker Zane Gonzalez missed two field goals and an extra point, leaving seven points on the field in a two-point loss. Like I said, bad teams find ways to lose. Takeaway: What happened to Houston's defense? Yes, C.J. Stroud and the Texans offense deserve plenty of blame. Here's what that unit did in the second half: punt, punt, punt, punt, touchdown, punt, punt, turnover on downs. Outside of the one touchdown drive, Houston gained just 11 yards on its other seven possessions. All that being said, the offense gave the defense a 17-0 lead against Deshaun Watson and the Cleveland Browns. Honestly, that should have been enough; this was one of the best defenses in the NFL last season. Instead, they allowed 27 points over the final three quarters and a game-winning touchdown drive in the final two minutes. Credit to Watson for once again showing up in crunch time, but head coach DeMeco Ryans, known as a defensive genius, should find his seat very, very warm after this start to the season, particularly on defense. Takeaway: Someone has to win the NFC South, and the Panthers are now in control. This game had a tremendous ending, though neither team played particularly well. The teams combined for 20 points in the final four minutes, including Ryan Fitzgerald's game-winning 54-yard field goal as time expired. But the Panthers committed a ridiculous 17 penalties for 152 yards, the Saints turned the ball over twice and the teams combined for just 407 total yards through the first 56 minutes. Carolina now leads the NFC South, which appears to be a battle for which team gets to lose at home in the wild-card round. Takeaway: Survive and advance. I wrote earlier this week that the Rams just needed to survive long enough for Puka Nacua and Davante Adams to get healthy and return to the lineup. They had no problem doing exactly that against a bad Cardinals team. The offense looked explosive, and the defense forced multiple turnovers. The problem is that the easy stretch of the schedule is over after four straight wins over the Raiders, Chargers, Commanders and Cardinals. After next week's bye, the Rams face the Packers, Chiefs and 49ers. If the Rams can sneak into the playoffs, they're a potentially dangerous team. But the upcoming stretch is going to determine whether that's possible. Takeaway: Fernando Mendoza at least makes the Raiders more interesting. Mendoza made his first career NFL start after Las Vegas traded Kirk Cousins to Minnesota following Week 9. He wasn't able to lead the team to a victory, but there were plenty of positives to take from the start. Mendoza adds a rushing element to the Raiders offense that didn't exist under Cousins. He used his feet to pick up yards and extend plays while looking downfield. The offense looked good on its first couple of drives, but a first-quarter ankle injury to star tight end Brock Bowers left the rookie without his best weapon for the second half. One thing Mendoza needs to learn quickly, though, is when a play is over. The rookie took some big hits when he'd have been better off sliding or getting out of bounds. Takeaway: I'm running out of ways to say the 49ers are really good. San Francisco has dealt with a litany of injuries this season but hasn't missed a beat. The 49ers traded for Keenan Allen to shore up a wide receiver group hit particularly hard by the injury bug, and he made an immediate impact with four catches for 53 yards in his first half as a 49er. Deebo Samuel returned from injury and had a 70-yard touchdown run on a reverse. Christian McCaffrey finished with 223 yards from scrimmage and three touchdowns, including touchdown catches of 74 and 66 yards. And backup running back Kaelon Black trucked two Cowboys defenders on a 25-yard touchdown run. Black's presence has allowed San Francisco to manage McCaffrey's workload, helping keep the veteran fresh for a potential Super Bowl run. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Brock Purdy is playing like an MVP and deserves significant consideration for the award. Through nine games, the 49ers have spent nearly 371 minutes leading and just 81 minutes trailing. That's more than four and a half times as much time playing from ahead as playing from behind. San Francisco has the inside track for the No. 1 seed in the NFC, and it's hard to imagine many teams capable of going into Levi's Stadium and beating this squad in January. Takeaway: When Cincinnati plays like that, there's no team in the NFL that can beat them. The Bengals' performance against the Steelers on Sunday Night Football was a masterclass in how to play football. Period. Heading into the fourth quarter, Cincinnati had outgained Pittsburgh 423-34. Joe Burrow had as many completions (34) as the Steelers had total yards. And here's the part that should worry the rest of the league: the problems that plagued the Bengals in recent seasons don't seem to exist right now. The question was never whether Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are good enough to lead a Super Bowl offense. The question was whether the offensive line could give Burrow enough time to find those two stars. Well, against one of the best defensive fronts in the NFL, the Bengals offensive line completely dominated. Through three quarters, Pittsburgh had managed just one sack, and Burrow had 366 passing yards. The other question was whether the defense could get enough stops. Now, Pittsburgh's offense certainly isn't elite. Still, the Bengals stonewalled the run, pressured Aaron Rodgers and made plays on the ball the few times he had enough time to throw it. The Steelers entered the fourth quarter with just 2 net passing yards. The Bengals' best is simply better than any other team's best.

items.summary: Peter Stylianou’s watchably unsettling tale of unbalanced minds and Unidentified Aerial Phenomena does its best to please Drone shots are two-a-penny in cinema these days, but it’s a mark of this £80,000 British indie sci-fi’s visual astuteness that it largely avoids them in a film plagued by drone-like entities. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank. Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Already not at ease among his mates, Kate gets a ribbing when she repeats her UFO story (or Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, as they are called these days). And there are knowing glances about her psychiatric history: she once fended off an abusive boyfriend at knifepoint, insisting he was possessed. But if she is delusional, then it seems to be spreading: her one ally, spacey teacher Shelly (Ayvianna Snow), re-enters the room after a suspiciously long fag break, marvelling about how they will all imminently join “the light”.

items.originalTitle: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.author: Duncan Riddell
items.title: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.summary: The latest in our series of writers picking their most comforting rewatches is a tribute to Curtis Hanson’s insightful 2000 comedy drama I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all. I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Even the misadventures of the film’s professor, Grady Tripp (Michael Douglas, never better), seemed romantic to me. On the eve of his university’s annual literary festival, Grady’s wife leaves him. His lover, Sara, announces she’s pregnant with his child. And James Leer, his brilliant but troubled student, who can rattle off Hollywood suicides in alphabetical order, shows up at the festival’s kick-off party cradling what may or may not be a cap gun. Grady responds to all this with the urgency of a veteran pot smoker – which he is.

items.originalTitle: Democrats Call for Probe Into Military Leaders as U.S. Army Whistleblower Alleges Warnings Were Dismissed Ahead of Deadly Iran Attack
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
items.title: Democrats Call for Probe Into Military Leaders as U.S. Army Whistleblower Alleges Warnings Were Dismissed Ahead of Deadly Iran Attack
items.summary: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth salutes as a U.S. Army carry team moves a flag-draped transfer case containing the remains of Sgt. 1st Class Noah L. Tietjens at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on March 7, 2026. —Roberto Schmidt—Getty Images An American soldier has alleged that U.S. military leaders dismissed concerns ahead of an Iranian attack that killed six servicemembers on March 1. The complaint, submitted Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS on Sunday, alleges that U.S. Army leaders did not heed warnings about thin fortifications at a command post at Kuwait’s Port Shuaiba. Iran launched a retaliatory drone attack on the command post a day after the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28. It remains the deadliest attack on American troops since 2021. Over the eight months of the war, a total of 23 U.S. servicemembers have died . Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, who filed the complaint and was among the dozens wounded in the attack, called the event a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.” Ramsbottom said he had twice raised concerns about the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors but was told, “We don’t have to worry about protection.” He said in an interview with CBS that a counter-drone system “never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested.” He also alleged that the post had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance.” A day after the attack, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the command post suffered casualties despite its fortifications not because of a lack of preparedness. “Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through [air defenses]. And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified,” Hegseth said at a press conference. “But these are powerful weapons.” The Pentagon announced an investigation into the attack on March 3, and the Associated Press reported that it had concluded in June, with a private briefing to families of the slain servicemembers in July. The findings of the investigation have not been publicly disclosed, although widow Michelle Tietjens told CBS that officials acknowledged no mistakes. Ramsbottom’s attorneys separately requested an independent investigation into the attack after filing his Nov. 13 complaint. TIME has reached out to the Pentagon and U.S. Central Command for comment. Disputed accounts Around a week before the U.S. and Israel launched their attacks on Iran, around 70 members of the U.S. Army’s 103rd Sustainment Command were relocated from Camp Arifjan, a major U.S. base south of Kuwait City, to the smaller outpost at Port of Shuaiba. Days after the war began, Hegseth told reporters that the Defense Department prioritized protecting U.S. troops and moving “the vast majority … off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire.” The facility, situated in the civilian port on Kuwait’s southern coast, was within range of Iranian missiles. The Washington Post reported in July that military leaders had ignored intelligence warnings that the post was a probable Iranian target. CBS reported in March that the post was surrounded by T-walls, steel-reinforced concrete barriers that provide protection from mortars and rockets. Ramsbottom told Colorado news station KOAA in April that the facility was protected from “legacy threats” like mortar fire and car bombs, but not from modern aerial attacks, such as by drones or missiles. Other survivors of the attack told CBS in April that the unit “was unprepared to provide any defense for itself. It was not a fortified position.” One soldier described the fort as “a bunch of little tin buildings where we can set up makeshift offices.” The Post reported that a 2021 photograph showed what appeared to be a thin metal rooftop over the building, although it was not clear whether any reinforcement existed underneath. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell rejected reporting that the position was not well-protected. “A Tactical Operations Center is not a ‘makeshift office space.’ The secure facility was fortified with 6-foot walls,” he posted on March 3. “Every possible measure has been taken to safeguard our troops — at every level,” Parnell wrote. Multiple news outlets previously reported that no sirens sounded to alert troops before the deadly strike. CBS reported in March that sirens had occasionally gone off after a drone had already entered the base in previous incidents. CBS reported in April that incoming missile alarms had sounded several hours before the attack, alerting around 60 troops to take cover when a ballistic missile flew overhead, and that an all-clear alert had sounded around 30 minutes before the Iranian drone hit. Troops told the outlet that officers had removed their helmets and resumed work at their desks after the all-clear alert. Soldiers told the Post that the threat warning system was initially not working when a team was sent to scout the post before troops were relocated there. They said repairs had been made to get it operational before the strike happened. U.S. Army Central previously said in statements to media outlets that the alarm system at the facility was working at the time of the attack. Democrats call for probe The whistleblower complaint adds fuel to the fire as Democrats plan to launch congressional investigations into the Trump Administration’s handling of the war when they take control of both chambers of Congress in January. In September, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York called for public hearings, citing earlier whistleblower reports about delayed medical care for wounded servicemembers, mistreatment of families, and concerns around the Army’s investigation into the attack. Rep. Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire described the handling of the attack as “a profound failure of leadership” and said “the Pentagon cannot be allowed to stonewall Congress.” Democrats and some Republicans have also called for Hegseth to step down or face impeachment , and the latest allegations are likely to intensify scrutiny of his leadership. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D, Conn.), the ranking member on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reportedly sent a letter on Sunday to the Pentagon requesting a classified briefing with Hegseth and “all force protection assessments” for the post. “I’m again demanding full disclosure about the Port Shuaiba attack—an accounting of misjudgments by political appointees likely led to increased vulnerability & greater casualties,” Blumenthal posted on social media on Sunday night. “The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, & the American people deserve full transparency & accountability,” he added in another post . “It is time for a reckoning.”

items.originalTitle: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
items.author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
items.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
items.summary: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

items.originalTitle: Being single can be a gift. Here’s how to embrace it.
items.author: Casper ter Kuile
items.title: Being single can be a gift. Here’s how to embrace it.
items.summary: When you’re single, it’s hard to avoid questions about your dating life. “Are you seeing anyone?” people will ask. “Had any fun dates?” Well-meant as it may be, these questions can leave you feeling less than, like you’ve failed in something that you were supposed to have figured out by now. At their worst, frequent questions about your love life imply that you don’t have love at all. Because we all learn, sooner or later, that there’s an expected direction of travel in life: Get an education; then a job. Fall in love and get married. Buy a house. Have children. And, of course, if you tick all those boxes, the expectation is that you’ll live happily ever after. Our rational brains understand this is just a fairy tale. But the gravitational pull of its mythic expectations can feel impossible to withstand — hence those questions as you catch up with friends at happy hour or pass the cranberry sauce during the holidays. And it isn’t just social pressure; there are numerous policies and tax breaks that incentivize marriage and children . The architecture of our society is built for couples, so if you’re single — whether by choice or by circumstance — how should you live? Who better to ask than a nun? Anne Curtis is a Sister of Mercy and the executive director of Mercy by the Sea , a retreat center in Madison, Connecticut. As a young woman, she made a vow to dedicate her life to God, which meant remaining single; it didn’t mean withdrawing from love — but allowing for more of it. If you’re imagining a stern old lady dressed in a habit, let me quickly disabuse you of that notion. For starters, Curtis, like most American nuns today, wears regular clothes. And she’s spent her life putting love for others into action. She campaigned for a living wage, affordable housing, and environmental protections through Network , a Catholic social justice lobbying group, and represented American nuns during a period of highly publicized tension with the more conservative Vatican. In her, I see a model of singlehood that challenges the assumptions many of us have about being unpartnered, and the pervasive idea that coupledom equals love and singledom equals loneliness. First, Curtis has lived and worked among her community of sisters since entering the novitiate decades ago, building deep friendships. Second, without a partner, Curtis has been able to offer much more love to her family and friends, especially in times of trial. “One of my sisters lost her spouse three years ago, and to this day, we check in every single day,” she says. “Just a really quick text. It’s part of, for me, entering into the day…. I sit in quiet, I pray, I walk the land here, I text my sister. I have a whole list of people who I specifically remember each day in my own prayer and reflection, because of something they’ve asked or some need they have.” When I ask if she gives more love than she receives, Curtis challenges the assumptions of the question: “The more that I’ve understood and come in touch with the fact that I was created and came out of love, then I’m also able to offer that love [to others]. And it’s responded to.” The work of her faith is to ground herself in that reality. “The more genuine and authentic I am, the more love I experience,” she says. This experience of belovedness enables Curtis to carry an awareness of, and tend to, the larger needs of the world. “I stand at the threshold of the land and the water and the sky,” she says. “I’m so aware of the expanse of the universe all around me and the worlds of Palestine, Ukraine, Sudan, Ethiopia. So many places where there’s incredible turmoil. And, I feel like, because of my life, I belong to a worldwide family.” Of course, her life isn’t always easy. “When we say yes to something, we say no to a whole lot of other things,” she says. “It would be a lie to say I never felt the loneliness of my life choice or to say ‘I wonder what my life would have been like if…’” Particularly in her younger years, she found it difficult. But, with time, she realized this yearning was just part of the process — and it was wise to embrace what she had in all its joys and its struggles. “At some point in your life, it’s important to say yes to something,” she says. James Martin understands this equally well. He’s a Jesuit priest and editor-at-large of America magazine. Similar to Curtis, he, too, took a vow of chastity and has therefore lived as a single person, a journey he documents in his memoir Work in Progress . Although he affirms that the Catholic Church actively promotes marriage, the “more basic is the idea that we’re meant for love.” Think about that: Humans are designed for connection — and the way that love is given and received is different for each person, Martin says. Whether you find that in a partnership, in a community, in a family, or in service, what matters, according to this Catholic tradition, is that we love and are loved in return. Should anyone doubt that, Martin laughs and says, “Let me just remind you…Jesus was single!” “God calls us to be who we are,” Martin says. “You are called to be yourself in all of your beauty.” The question to ask, he says, is “How can I live out that calling in a loving way, and in a fruitful way and in a way that will help me to — one of my favorite words from Thomas Aquinas — help me to flourish?” Martin does this in his own life via the Daily Examen . The Examen is a roughly 500-year-old prayer practice developed by the founder of the Jesuit order, St. Ignatius of Loyola. At the end of a day, maybe as you lay down to sleep, you go through your day hour by hour to notice the presence of God. If the word God gets in your way, try asking yourself, “Where did I notice love today?” It might be in the smile exchanged with a baby in the grocery aisle, while planning a friend’s birthday dinner, or getting a hug from your mom. If you’ve never tried it before, give it a go. It’s a powerful practice of gratitude and trains you to notice the beauty in your life. In my experience, the Examen helps me practice what Martin describes as having what you have, rather than focusing on what you don’t. Naturally, that shift can take time. Brianna Cayo Cotter, a social impact executive in her 40s who is single, has noticed this change over decades, too. “In my 20s, I was dating lots of different people,” she says, “figuring out…heartbreak and highs and lows.” Then, in her 30s, she felt a longing and a yearning as she saw a lot of people coupling off. “And that felt…like a loss at the time.” But now she’s come to a great acceptance — partly because she’s seen that marriage is no guarantee to stave off loneliness, and comes with many of its own burdens. “I think my life is actually better and more rich and has more love and companionship in it than most of the couples that I know,” she says. “Not all! But, really most.” So many coupled friends struggle to build community in their forties, for example. “I can empathize, but I cannot relate at all.” But more than this, being single gives Cayo Cotter more time. “More time in your life to be juicy and spread more love and deepen it and have profoundly intimate relationships with lots of different people in different ways.” Whether she’s traveling with others, hosting friends, or getting together with neighbors on her block, Cayo Cotter lives a life in which she is wildly loved. Of course, she still gets those questions. “I remember my mom, when she was visiting me one time, she was like, ‘But who would go and pick you up when you get your colonoscopy?’” Cayo Cotter says with a laugh. “I was like, ‘I could ask 20 people to do that!’” Because she gives love so generously, she receives it bountifully, too. And despite not being a nun, or even religiously affiliated, this practice of loving and being loved has a spiritual quality for Cayo Cotter. She practices yoga daily, and says one closing prayer really resonates with her: “ The light in me sees the light in you . And the more that you can go out into the world with a greater light shining from you… that is how to live.” Curtis would agree: “Whatever your faith dimension is or practice or belief, I think they all, in some way, are a call to love. … There’s limitless ways to offer love and be loved.” So when people ask whether you’re dating anyone, you might want to answer the bigger question that they’re prodding for: “No, I’m not partnered. But I am very loved.”

items.title: The Hypocrisy of Anthropic’s IPO
items.summary: Until fairly recently, Anthropic was best known as OpenAI’s quirky, safety-minded junior competitor, founded by breakaway OpenAI staff who believed that their former employer was pushing AI development too recklessly in pursuit of profits. Now the company is on the verge of becoming one of the most valuable on the stock market. Anthropic plans to go public on Wednesday at a valuation of $1.4 trillion. It promises investors that it will generate huge returns by relentlessly pursuing the very strategies that its leaders and employees believe could lead to superintelligent AI wiping out all of humanity. Anthropic’s stated commitment to safety has always existed in tension with its pursuit of profit. Its IPO is a clear sign that the pursuit of profit is winning. Anthropic’s business model is based on having the most sophisticated AI models and charging businesses a lot for their use. The company’s Claude products, especially the software-development tool Claude Code, are widely considered the best on the market, and companies have lined up to pay for them. Over the past year, Anthropic’s quarterly revenue has increased more than tenfold, from $1.4 billion to $17 billion—more than six times the rate that Google’s and Meta’s revenues rose in the year leading up to their IPOs. It began turning a profit in the second quarter of 2026. But, as the company acknowledges in the “risk factors” section of its IPO filing, its further growth hinges on staying ahead of the competition. Revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of this year, largely because OpenAI and Chinese companies released models nearly as capable as Claude, eating into Anthropic’s market share. “Anthropic really can’t afford to stand still,” Jay Ritter, the director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida, told me. “If they stumble, the industry could end up in a situation like with airplanes, where Boeing and Airbus engage in price wars and neither ends up very profitable.” To preserve its advantage, Anthropic has made roughly $900 billion in commitments to purchase the chips and build the data centers that it needs in order to keep improving its models. About half of that bill comes due before 2030. Private money from a handful of institutional investors simply isn’t enough to fund that kind of spending binge. So Anthropic is turning to public markets instead. [ Rogé Karma: Democrats have no coherent plan for AI ] Anthropic’s plan for all that money revolves around using current AI to build better future AI, which will in turn create even better versions of itself, and so on—a process known as recursive self-improvement. The company is explicit that achieving this milestone first is its big bet. “If our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind,” its IPO filing explains. But in the very same document, Anthropic acknowledges that recursive self-improvement could cause immense and perhaps even apocalyptic harm. “Concerns have been raised,” it states, “that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” The document goes on to argue that “these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development.” Translation: The approach that we’ve staked our business on might be the thing that ends up killing us all. Whether recursive self-improvement can in fact be achieved in the near future, if at all, and whether it really would pose an existential risk to humanity, are very much up for debate. What is clear is that Anthropic’s leaders and many of its employees believe both propositions to be true; they are the ones who have raised the concerns. In a September essay , CEO Dario Amodel warned that AI systems were advancing so quickly that “in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.” He concluded that recursive self-improvement “must be pursued very carefully, if at all.” Several employees have recently resigned in order to warn against what they believe to be the escalating risk of disaster. Anthropic did not respond to interview requests. But it has publicly articulated a justification for the seeming contradiction between its warnings about AI safety and its relentless efforts to make AI more powerful. Its leadership argues that, absent some kind of international agreement, somebody is going to build superintelligent AI. Better for Anthropic to get there first, while using its clout to push the entire AI industry toward placing safety over profits—an approach that the company calls “race to the top.” As proof of their sincerity, Anthropic’s leaders cite the company’s April decision to delay the public release of its Mythos model to give major companies and governments time to strengthen their cybersecurity. They also point to the company’s refusal to allow the Pentagon to use Anthropic’s tools to conduct mass surveillance or develop autonomous weapons. “We have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line," Amodei recently wrote on X, adding that “I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.” But in other cases, Anthropic seems to have allowed its financial incentives to outweigh its safety considerations. As Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode, an AI-focused think tank, recently pointed out , the company has lobbied to defeat or significantly water down legislation that would impose stricter safety standards on the AI industry. In October, in response to a wave of federal legislative proposals to regulate the industry, the company proposed a bill that would set an almost impossibly high bar for the federal government to block deployment of AI models and would preempt stricter state laws. “I just don’t think these are the kinds of actions a company would take if its main goal was to put safety first,” Calvin told me. “They seem much closer to how a company would act if it were trying to win the race to build superintelligence.” [ Read: Treat AI like a normal crisis ] The coming IPO will only make the pull of financial self-interest stronger. “The idea that this won’t impact people’s day-to-day decisions is ridiculous to me,” a former Anthropic employee, who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order not to jeopardize his career in AI, told me. “Even most altruistic people at the company will be checking the ticker every day.” When I asked Jay Ritter, the IPO expert, whether public shareholders in Anthropic should worry about the company choosing safety over returns, he made the same point. “I wouldn’t be too worried,” Ritter said. “We’ve seen time and time again that when management owns a lot of stock and employees own a lot of stock, they tend to act in ways that make the stock perform well.” To protect against this dynamic, Anthropic has created a unique governance structure in which a majority of its board is appointed not by the company’s leaders or shareholders, but by a “long-term benefit trust” composed of individuals who don’t have equity in the company and have been tasked with keeping the company’s safety mission in mind. But several legal experts have argued that this is unlikely to stop the company from prioritizing its financial goals. Roberto Tallarita, a Harvard Law professor who specializes in corporate governance, has pointed out that Anthropic’s governance structure allows a combination of employees, executives, and investors to vote to get rid of the trust altogether. “I give Anthropic a lot of credit for being creative about trying to insulate the company from financial pressure,” Tallarita told me. “But at the end of the day, if there ends up being a direct conflict between profits and safety, I just don’t think these mechanisms are strong enough on their own to make sure that safety wins out.” The possibility that AI systems will pursue different goals from the ones their human creators intend is known as the alignment problem. Anthropic, whose business incentive is at odds with its concern about AI safety, has an alignment problem of its own. To be fair to the company, in no other industry are private companies trusted to prioritize social values over their own bottom line. Amodei and other AI leaders correctly argue that only industry-wide regulation can restrict the pace of development . But this is yet another cause for concern about the Anthropic IPO. A major reason Donald Trump has refused to back any efforts to regulate AI is his fear of what they would do to the stock market. Adding another trillion-dollar company to the public markets will only heighten that fear. Anthropic’s alignment problem might soon become everyone else’s.
